title: Gujrat and annexation, 1849
hook: the last battle is lost, the soldiers lay down their arms, and the Punjab is annexed

segments.voice: Yesterday, Chillianwala, and your line was they held. Where did you stay put for one breath longer? Today, the holding ends. Day nine hundred thirty-nine.

A line of soldiers comes forward, one by one, and lays down its weapons on a pile. Swords, matchlocks, shields. These are men of the Khalsa army, and the war is over. There's a story told about that day. An old soldier, setting down his arms, says quietly that today Ranjit Singh has died. The Maharaja was long dead. But the kingdom he built was ending in front of them. Today: Gujrat and annexation.
screen: `WEAPONS LAID ON A PILE.` → `TODAY RANJIT SINGH HAS DIED.` → `A KINGDOM ENDING.`

segments.voice: First, the battle. Gujrat here is a town in the Punjab, not the Indian state of a similar name. After Chillianwala, the British waited for more troops, and above all more heavy guns. At Gujrat they used them. A long, heavy bombardment came before the infantry moved, and this time the Sikh line broke. Second, the surrender. The British pursued the retreating army. Its leaders, Sher Singh Attariwala and his father Chattar Singh, gave themselves up, and the soldiers handed over their arms. That's where the story of the old soldier is set. It may be remembered more than recorded, but Sikhs have kept telling it because it says what the day meant. Third, the annexation. Lord Dalhousie did not restore the court at Lahore. He declared the Punjab part of British India. The boy Maharaja, Duleep Singh, still a child, was made to put his name to terms that gave up his kingdom and his claims to it. The flag over the fort at Lahore was changed. Fourth, what Sikh scripture says about endings. In his saloks near the close of the Guru Granth Sahib, Guru Tegh Bahadur describes a person whose strength has gone, who is bound and can find no way out. And in the next breath the verse turns: strength returns, the bonds fall away, and everything is in the Lord's hands. The Guru doesn't pretend the binding isn't real. He just doesn't stop the verse there. A kingdom did end at Gujrat, and the story of the old soldier doesn't hide it. That's today's line.
screen: `THE GUNS AT GUJRAT.` · `THE ARMS LAID DOWN.` · `THE PUNJAB ANNEXED.` · `BOUND, AND THEN THE VERSE TURNS.` · then, large: `THE KINGDOM ENDED.`

segments.voice: Two minutes with an ending. Sit, and let your shoulders drop. Bring to mind one thing in your life that is over and won't come back: a school you left, a team you played on, a routine you shared with someone, a version of yourself. Don't argue with it, and don't dress it up. Just let it be what it was. Notice where you feel it in your body. Breathe into that place, slowly, three or four times, and then keep breathing at your own pace. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.

Bandhan, bonds. Guru Tegh Bahadur's salok speaks of being bound, and then of the bonds falling away, as the last battle was lost to the big guns and the Punjab declared part of British India. Today's word.
Your line: the kingdom ended. Today, sit with one ending honestly for a minute, without rushing to fix it. Day nine hundred thirty-nine.

howItsDone: Sikh histories mark the defeat at Gujrat and the annexation that followed as the end of the Sikh kingdom of the Punjab, and the story of the soldiers laying down their arms is still told at gatherings about that history.
